title: Tara
hookLine: Green Tara, the bodhisattva who acts swiftly to protect

lines: A CAR ON ICE. A FEVER AT 3 A.M.
A WOMAN ON A LOTUS, GREEN.
cards: A car sliding on ice. A child with a fever at three in the morning. When you're really scared, you don't want a long lecture.
You want someone who comes quickly. Now picture a painting on a Tibetan wall: a woman seated on a lotus, her body green like young leaves. Her left leg is folded in meditation.
Her right leg is stretched out, foot already stepping down off the seat, as if she's heard you and is on her way.

teach.h: TARA — STAR, AND THE ONE WHO FERRIES.
teach.b: Tara, whom Tibetans call Dolma, is one of the best-loved figures in Tibetan Buddhism. Her name has two meanings in Sanskrit: star, the light you steer by, and she who carries across, like a ferry over a river.

teach.h: BORN FROM A TEAR OF COMPASSION.
teach.b: A well-known story says she was born from compassion itself. Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva you met in the Heart Sutra and in the six syllables, looked at the suffering of the world and wept.
Where a tear fell, a lotus grew, and from the lotus rose Tara.
Another story, told in a later Tibetan history, is about a princess named Wisdom Moon who practiced so deeply that monks advised her to pray for rebirth as a man, to reach awakening.
She answered that in the deepest sense there is no man or woman to cling to, and she vowed to keep working for beings in a woman's form until all are free. There are many Taras.
White Tara is linked with long life and healing. Green Tara is swift, active protection, and that stepping-down foot is the whole point: compassion that doesn't wait.
A well-known hymn praises twenty-one forms of Tara, and many Tibetans chant it every morning.
Tradition says she protects from eight fears: lions, elephants, fire, snakes, thieves, prison, floods and demons.
Later teachers read those inwardly too: pride, confusion, anger, envy, wrong views, greed, clinging and doubt.
Many Tibetans turn to her in any trouble, big or small, and trust her the way you'd trust someone who picks up on the first ring.

how: Many Tibetan Buddhists recite Tara's mantra and the Praise to the Twenty-One Taras daily, turn to Green Tara in times of danger or fear, and keep her image on household shrines.

p: star; the one who ferries across

s: Green Tara's right foot is stepping down off her seat
it shows compassion that doesn't wait: she's already on her way.
a story says Tara was born from Avalokiteshvara's tear
where the tear fell a lotus grew, and from it rose Tara.
there are many; a well-known hymn praises twenty-one.

games.q: you're the princess Wisdom Moon. the monks advise you to pray for rebirth as a man so you can reach awakening. what do you answer?
o: say there's no man or woman to cling to, and vow to work in a woman's form.
games.why: in the story she vows to keep working for beings in a woman's form until all are free, and becomes Tara.

practice: Picture a quick, kind helper settling beside you: Green Tara, green as new leaves, one foot stepping toward you, or someone from your own life who always came when you called.
Then turn it around, and imagine being that quick, kind helper for someone else. Let the picture fade, and rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Tara. The star, the one who ferries across: in Tibetan Buddhism, the bodhisattva of swift compassion, one foot already stepping down.

orig.note: Sanskrit tārā: star, and she who carries across. Tibetan: Dolma (sgrol ma), 'she who frees'.

carryVoice: Your line: she comes quickly. Compassion that doesn't wait. Rest well, and come back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taranatha, The Golden Rosary (history of the Tara tantra), the story of Wisdom Moon
